title: Queen against rook II: how to reach Philidor
summary: From the second rank to Philidor: the king enters from the side, the queen takes away the rook's checks, the triple threat and a game from 1992.
history: Last lesson you won from Philidor's position; the hard part is getting there. A 1958 position by former world champion Max Euwe shows how to break down the rook that defends beside its king. In 2002 grandmaster John Nunn split the ending into four phases: first, bring the king and drive the enemy king to an edge; then break the rook's defences on the fourth, the third and finally the second rank, which leads to Philidor. This lesson shows the first phase and the last; the ones in between are for the next lesson. In 1992, at a tournament in Germany, the Icelander Hannes Stefánsson drove Karsten Müller's king from the middle of the board to the corner and captured the rook; Nunn remarked that he did not always find the shortest way, but played precisely and logically.
part.diagonal.title: The diagonal position
part.diagonal.summary: Four pieces on one diagonal: a queen triangle passes the move and the discovered check leads to Philidor.
step.t_diagonal: Last lesson you won from Philidor. Today is the road there, and we start with the position closest to it. Queen, our king, rook and black king stand in a row on the diagonal from e5 to b8. If our king leaves d6 once the rook is no longer on c7, the queen gives a discovered check. With Black to move, every move makes things worse for Black; but it is our move. Which sequence gives back this same position with Black to move, and how does it end in Philidor?
step.t_diagonal.hint1: The position is fine. What is wrong is whose move it is.
step.t_diagonal.hint2: Last lesson the queen lost a move by walking a triangle, without changing anything on the board.
step.diagonal: This is the diagonal position, as Unto's training position presents it. The rook is caught between two dangers: if it leaves the diagonal, our king steps aside with a discovered check and the black king goes to the corner; if it moves along the c-file, it loses quickly. That is why we want Black to move. The queen loses a move in three moves: she steps back along the same diagonal, gives a check and returns. It is the triangle from last lesson.
step.d_diagonal.m1: 1.Qf4! The queen steps back along the same diagonal. She stays behind our king, and the battery aimed at b8 stays in place.
step.d_diagonal.m2: 1...Kc8. Black's best: the king leaves the diagonal before it turns into a weapon.
step.d_diagonal.m3: 2.Qf5+. A check along the c8 diagonal sends the king back.
step.d_diagonal.m4: 2...Kb8. Back on the diagonal, the safest square he has.
step.d_diagonal.m5: 3.Qe5. The starting position again, now with Black to move. That is the move the queen lost.
step.d_diagonal.m6: 3...Rb7. The rook leaves the diagonal, because every other move loses faster. The road for the discovered check is open.
step.discover: Now, after 3.Qe5 Rb7, only our king stands between the queen and the black king. Finish it: the king steps out with a discovered check, and the queen reaches Philidor.
step.discover.hint: The king leaves the diagonal next to the rook. Then the queen works along the a-file.
step.discover.done: 4.Kc6+ Ka8 5.Qa1+ Kb8 6.Qa5 is Philidor, with Black to move: six moves from the diagonal position.
part.second.title: The second-rank defence
part.second.summary: The rook cuts our king off on the rank next to the black king. One check, and the king comes in from the side, not from the front.
step.t_second: One step back. The black king is on the edge and the rook, on the rank next to it, cuts our king off: he cannot cross to the seventh rank. If Black were to move, the rook could still check from b7 and from e6. This is the second-rank defence. What are the first two moves to break it?
step.t_second.hint1: A queen check first, to drive the black king off c8.
step.t_second.hint2: Then the king. He does not go in front of the black king: look at what the rook would do along the sixth rank.
step.intro: This is Euwe's position, from 1958. The rook on e7 guards the black king from the side and closes the seventh rank to our king. The goal is Philidor: the black king stuck on the edge, the rook beside him and our king a knight's jump away. For that our king has to come in, and the right road is from the side, away from the rank where the rook can check.
step.d_kc6: First, the road that looks shortest and is not.
step.d_kc6.m1: 1.Qf5+. The check along the diagonal drives the black king off c8.
step.d_kc6.m2: 1...Kd8. The king goes to d8, next to the rook.
step.d_kc6.m3: 2.Kc6? The king goes forward, towards d6. It looks direct, but it stops on the sixth rank, and the rook can reach e6.
step.d_kc6.m4: 2...Re6+! The rook checks and leaves the second rank. After 3.Kd5, 3...Ra6 settles the rook on the third rank, the most stubborn barrier of this ending and the subject of the next lesson. It still wins, but it costs three moves and a harder defence.
step.open: Now the right way. You have already seen the check; after it, find the king square where he is not exposed to the rook's checks.
step.open.hint: After the check, the king goes sideways, on the fifth rank, and not to c6.
step.open.done: 1.Qf5+ Kd8 2.Kc5! On c5 the rook has no useful check, and the black king has to choose which side to go.
part.kingBack.title: The black king comes back
part.kingBack.summary: A check to gain time, the king one step forward, along the b-file. And a game from 1992 that got here.
step.t_kingBack: After 1.Qf5+ Kd8 2.Kc5, the toughest defence is 2...Kc7: the black king goes back next to the rook. Our king wants to get close to him to set up Philidor, and the rook still watches the e-file and the seventh rank. What is the plan: which way does our king go, and what does the queen do before each of his steps?
step.t_kingBack.hint1: The queen takes squares away before the king moves. When she checks, it is to gain time.
step.t_kingBack.hint2: The king goes round one side, along the b-file, not through the middle.
step.hannes: Where this plan leads: this position came up in a real game, Hannes Stefánsson against Karsten Müller, in Altensteig, Germany, in 1992. The game began as a French Defence; on move 71 only queen against rook was left, and seventeen moves later the two reached exactly this position: our king on b5, facing the black king, and the queen behind everything, on e8. Stefánsson set up Philidor on move 92; Müller still tried 92...Rb1, the escape from last lesson, and lost the rook on move 98. Now see how to get here when the black king comes back.
step.d_kingBack: The pattern of the whole lesson: the queen gains a move, the king takes a step.
step.d_kingBack.m1: 3.Qd5! The queen goes to the centre without checking. From d5 she eyes b7, c6 and d7, the squares around the black king.
step.d_kingBack.m2: 3...Rd7. The rook attacks the queen and stays right next to the black king, on the seventh rank.
step.d_kingBack.m3: 4.Qe5+. A check to gain time: the black king has to leave c7.
step.d_kingBack.m4: 4...Kb7. The king goes to b7, closer to the corner.
step.m_kingBack: Your turn. The rook is on d7, and the black king reached b7 after 4.Qe5+ Kb7. Take the king's step, then close the last rank with the queen.
step.m_kingBack.hint: The king goes round along the b-file; then the queen goes behind everything, on the eighth rank.
step.m_kingBack.done: 5.Kb5 Rc7 6.Qe8! On b5 our king faces the black king and takes a6, b6 and c6 away from him; from e8 the queen watches the eighth rank and d7, and the black king only has a7. It is the position from Stefánsson's game.
part.stalemate.title: Beware of stalemate
part.stalemate.summary: Near the corner, the rook offers itself with check. Before putting the king on a square, count the black king's squares.
step.t_stalemate: The black king is on the edge, with the rook beside him, and our king has already reached c6. It looks like time to put the king on b6, a knight's jump from the black king, as in Philidor. Before you play, look at the black king's squares and at the checks the rook still has. Which move wins without giving Black a chance?
step.t_stalemate.hint1: Picture the king on b6. Which check would the rook have, and what would it attack at the same time?
step.t_stalemate.hint2: If the queen captures the rook and the black king has no move, it is a draw. Look for a queen move that leaves the rook unable to move.
step.stale: What changes: until now the danger was the rook's checks; now it is the black king running out of moves. The natural move, 1.Kb6?, is exactly the mistake. On b6 our king stands on the same rank as the queen, and the rook can check along that rank, attacking both pieces at once. The king cannot reach the rook, so the queen has to capture, and then the black king has no square and is not in check: stalemate. The rook that offers itself with check when the black king has no square is the most common drawing weapon of this ending, near the corner. Before putting the king on a square, count the squares the black king would have after the capture.
step.d_trap: The trap, move by move. Our king has already gone to b6.
step.d_trap.m1: 1...Rd6+! The rook checks and attacks the queen along the sixth rank. If the king runs, the queen falls.
step.d_trap.m2: 2.Qxd6. The only capture, and the black king has no square and is not in check. A draw by stalemate.
step.m_pin: Now find the winning move. The king can wait; the queen first.
step.m_pin.hint: Look for the square from which the queen pins the rook to the black king, along the diagonal.
step.m_pin.done: 1.Qe6! pins the rook. It cannot leave d7 without exposing the king to check. After 1...Kb8 the rook is undefended, 2.Qxd7, and after 2...Ka8, 3.Qb7 is mate. 1.Qf5, on the same diagonal, also wins.
part.quiet.title: Before the king, take away the checks
part.quiet.summary: A quiet queen move is worth more than a check: she covers the rook's checking square or cuts off the rook that ran away.
step.t_quiet: Now the black king is on the other side, on g7, with the rook glued to him on f7. Our king wants to enter f6, but the rook greets him with checks. Nunn says the right move here is not obvious. What should the queen do before the king moves?
step.t_quiet.hint1: Picture the king on f6 and look for the checks the rook would have.
step.t_quiet.hint2: There is a square from which the queen watches g7 from far away.
step.quiet: This is a position from Nunn. What changes compared with the earlier parts: there the queen checked and the king advanced. Here a check leads nowhere, because the black king just shuffles between g7 and h7. The right idea is to prepare: the queen goes to a square from which she watches g7, the square from which the rook would check, and only then does the king come in. A quiet move that takes away the checks is worth more than a check.
step.d_quiet.m1: 1.Qd8. The queen keeps watching the eighth rank and opens the way down to the centre along the d-file.
step.d_quiet.m2: 1...Kh7. The king goes to h7, with the rook still glued to him.
step.d_quiet.m3: 2.Qd4! The move Nunn calls not obvious. From d4 the queen watches g7 along the diagonal. The rook still has the check on g7, but once it leaves, it cannot come back: g7 belongs to the queen.
step.d_quiet.m5: 3.Kf6. The king comes in attacking the rook. Against 3...Rg6+ comes 4.Kf7, and the checks are over: g7 belongs to the queen, and the rook is stuck next to its king.
step.d_loose: Now the same position, but Black moved first and the rook ran to f1, far from its king. Nunn recommends not chasing it with checks: with the rook cut off from its king, the queen blocks its way back.
step.d_loose.m1: 1.Qe5+. A check, and the black king chooses f7.
step.d_loose.m2: 1...Kf7. The king goes up to f7, in front of the rook.
step.d_loose.m3: 2.Qe3! The quiet move. From e3 the queen watches f2, f3, f4 and g1: the rook cannot check on g1, and if it goes back to its king with 2...Rf6, it falls after 3.Qa7+ Ke6 4.Qb6+ Ke5 5.Qxf6+.
step.d_loose.m4: 2...Ra1. The rook runs to the corner, far from everything. On its own, it is a target for a fork.
step.m_loose: The rook is on a1, alone. Now, yes, checks: each one pushes the black king until one of them also attacks the rook.
step.m_loose.hint: The checks drive the black king to the h8 corner. The fork comes along the long diagonal, which runs through a1.
step.m_loose.done: 3.Qf4+ Kg8 4.Qc4+ Kh7 5.Qf7+ Kh8 6.Qf6+ checks and attacks the rook along the diagonal to a1. It falls.
part.triple.title: The triple threat
part.triple.summary: A quiet move that threatens mate and the rook at the same time, and leaves the rook no good square.
step.t_triple: The black king is on the edge, on b8, and the rook has run to the middle of the board, to d5. Our king is already on a6, very close. Which queen move leaves Black without a single good move?
step.t_triple.hint1: First count the black king's squares. How many are left?
step.t_triple.hint2: If the queen took away his last square, what threat would be left hanging?
step.t_triple.hint3: And, from that same square, the queen can also look at the rook.
step.triple: What changes compared with the previous part: there the queen cut off the rook and then the checks came. Here one quiet move does it all at once. Nunn calls it the triple threat: the queen threatens mate, attacks the rook and leaves the rook no good square, because almost every rook move allows the mate.
step.d_triple.m1: 1.Qc6! The queen takes a8 away from the black king, who has no move left, threatens 2.Qb7 mate and attacks the rook on d5. Of the rook's fourteen squares, ten allow the mate; on the other four it is lost.
step.d_triple.m2: 1...Ra5+. The most stubborn defence: the rook offers itself with check, at least to escape the mate.
step.d_triple.m3: 2.Kxa5. The rook has fallen, and mate comes in a few moves.
step.m_triple: Now in another position. The black king is on c8, and the rook has run to a5. Find the triple threat.
step.m_triple.hint: A quiet queen move next to the black king, from where she threatens mate on c7 and looks at the rook.
step.m_triple.done: 1.Qb6! threatens 2.Qc7 mate and attacks a5. Against 1...Rc5, which guards c7 along the file, 2.Qxc5+ and the rook has fallen.
part.center.title: From the centre to the edge
part.center.summary: Back to the 1992 game: the check pushes the black king back, our king walks without checking and takes the space.
step.t_center: Back to the game between Stefánsson and Müller, eight moves before the position at the end of part 3. The black king is still in the middle, on c5, with the rook beside him; our king has already reached f5. Check or king move?
step.t_center.hint1: Checks alone lead nowhere: the black king just comes back to the centre.
step.t_center.hint2: The queen already closes the d-file. The one who needs to get close is our king.
step.center: Nunn puts this phase first: bring the king and push the black king to an edge. The rule: our king walks whenever he can, and the queen checks when the check sends the black king back and our king can take the square he left. Nunn remarked that Stefánsson did not always find the shortest way, but played precisely and logically.
step.d_center.m1: 81.Ke5. No check: our king takes the centre, next to the d-file that the queen already closes.
step.d_center.m2: 81...Kb6. The black king heads for the edge, and Müller sets up the third-rank defence, which you will see in the next lesson.
step.d_center.m3: 82.Qd4+. Now the check works: along the diagonal, it pushes the black king back.
step.d_center.m4: 82...Kb7. Nunn noted that 82...Kb5 held out five moves longer: near an edge the king defends better than in the corner.
step.m_center: Carry on like Stefánsson. The black king is on b7. Drive him to the last rank.
step.m_center.hint: The king advances one more step; then a check drives the black king to the eighth rank.
step.m_center.done: 83.Kd5 Rc7 84.Qb4+ Kc8 is the second rank, the defence from part 2 in another shape.
part.walk.title: Against the checks, the king goes closer
part.walk.summary: The king does not run from the rook's checks: he walks towards the black king, where the rook loses its squares. Then, the practical challenge.
step.t_walk: The same game, at move 85. It is the second rank, now with the rook on c7, glued to the black king. Stefánsson won from here, but Nunn found a shorter way. Our king has to reach c6 or d6, and the rook will check him on the way. How does the queen prepare the entry, and where does the king answer the checks?
step.t_walk.hint1: First a quiet queen move, without check.
step.t_walk.hint2: When the rook checks, the king does not retreat: he walks towards the black king.
step.walk: What changes: until now the rook stayed next to its king. Now it will check from close by. The rule holds for the whole ending: against the checks, our king walks towards the black king, because there the rook loses the squares it would check from. Running away from the checks only makes the game longer.
step.d_walk: First, what Stefánsson played: a longer road, but with the same rule.
step.d_walk.m1: 85.Qb5. A quiet move that takes b7 and b8 away from the black king.
step.d_walk.m2: 85...Rh7. The rook moves away from its king to get room for checks.
step.d_walk.m3: 86.Qe8+. A check along the eighth rank: the black king has to step up.
step.d_walk.m4: 86...Kb7. The king goes up to b7, near the corner, while the rook stays far from him, on h7.
step.d_walk.m5: 87.Kc5. Our king comes closer to the black king.
step.d_walk.m6: 87...Rc7+. The rook comes back and checks along the c-file.
step.d_walk.m7: 88.Kb5! The king answers the check by facing the black king, not by retreating. From here the game reached the position of part 3.
step.m_walk: Now Nunn's way, shorter. Play better than Stefánsson.
step.m_walk.hint: A quiet queen move that watches the diagonal up to e8. Then, against each check, the king walks closer to the black king.
step.m_walk.done: 85.Qa4! Rd7+ 86.Kc6 Rc7+ 87.Kd6. Twice the rook checked, and twice our king got closer to the black king. Now he is on d6, right next to the rook, and the defence is nearly broken.
step.recap: Three rules from this lesson. One: a check to gain time, the king one step forward, coming in from the side; and, near the corner, count the black king's squares before placing your king, because the rook offers itself with check. Two: before the king moves, a quiet queen move takes away the rook's checks or cuts it off from its king, and sometimes threatens three things at once. Three: our king walks whenever he can, towards the black king, even against the checks; the queen only checks when it pushes the black king back.
step.finish: Your turn in the practical challenge, from the second rank, Euwe's position. Start with the two moves from part 2 and see which defence Black chooses. If the rook runs away, cut it off before advancing the king.
practice: The second-rank defence, against the clock or without it. You know the first two moves by heart; from there, a check to gain time, the king one step forward, and Philidor.
ex.e12: A position from Nunn: the rook left the black king and has just gone to d1. Bring our king to the sixth rank without taking more checks.
ex.e12.hint: Before the king moves, a quiet queen move to the centre, from where she watches the b-file along both diagonals.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qe4 and, after 1...Rd7, 2.Kc6. From e4 the queen takes b7 and b1, and the rook loses the checks that mattered; the king enters on c6 attacking the rook, which goes back to b7. From there, 3.Qe8+ and 4.Qd8, and the position is Philidor's. It is the lesson's quiet-move idea: first the queen takes away the checks, then the king walks.
ex.e05: The black king is near the corner with the rook beside it. Find a queen move that gives the rook no check.
ex.e05.hint: The most natural check leaves the black king in the corner and our king with a single entry square. Look at what the rook does on that square.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Qe5 (or 1.Qd4). The queen stays far away and controls the central squares; the rook has no useful check. After 1.Qc6+ and 2.Kb6 the rook checks on a6 and any capture is stalemate: Berger's trap, from 1889.
ex.e13: Second-rank defence, but instead of guarding its king the rook ran away to e1, and three queen checks have already driven the black king to c8. Find the move that stops the rook from rejoining its king.
ex.e13.hint: Look at how the rook would come back: along the c-file or through the squares near its king. One queen square cuts off both.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Qc4! It is not a check: the queen takes the c-file and the diagonal to e2, and the rook cannot rejoin its king. From here the checks end in a fork: 1...Kc7 2.Qf4+ Kc8 3.Qg4+ Kd8 4.Qh4+, and the rook on e1 falls. More checks instead of 1.Qc4 only let the rook come back. The line is Max Euwe's.
ex.e14: The rook's other escape: after the check on f5 and the king on c5, the rook ran to e1 and the queen checked on d3. The rook will still give checks. Walk the king up to the black king without losing time.
ex.e14.hint: Our king climbs the d-file. The queen checks only to gain time, and one quiet queen move takes squares from the black king; when the rook checks, step towards the black king, not away from it.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd5, 2.Qf3+, 3.Qg4 (a quiet move), 4.Qf4+ and 5.Kd6. Against the checks, 6.Ke6 and 7.Kf6. With our king right next to the black king, the rook runs out of checks and falls to a fork: 7...Re2 8.Qa4+ and 9.Qd1+. The line is Max Euwe's.
ex.e15: Hannes Stefánsson against Karsten Müller, 1992: the black king is in the centre and the rook cuts our king off. In the game White played 74.Qe7 and lost four moves. Find the shortest way to the second-rank defence.
ex.e15.hint: A queen check along the fifth rank first; then our king walks, and the queen checks again only when the black king can be pushed to the seventh.
ex.e15.solution: 74.Qb5+, 75.Kg5, 76.Kf5, 77.Qb6+ and 78.Kf6. The check sends the black king back, our king climbs the f-file while the rook stays on the e-file, and the last check pushes the black king to the seventh rank. After 78...Kc8 79.Qa6+ Rb7 80.Ke6, it is the second rank from the lesson. The improvement is John Nunn's.
ex.e16: A position from Nunn: the black king went to the edge and the rook is far from it, on the h-file. Find the move that makes three threats at once.
ex.e16.hint: It is not a check. Look for a square from which the queen threatens mate and attacks the rook, and notice that the rook has no good check.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Qf8! It threatens 2.Qa8 mate and 2.Qxh6, and the rook's squares turn bad: almost every rook move allows the mate on a8. The most stubborn defence is 1...Rh5+; then the king goes to c6, and no further, to stop the checks. After 2...Ka7, 3.Qf7+ and the rook falls. Nunn calls it a "triple threat".
key.second: The black rook defends beside its king, on the second rank, and looks solid. With a well-chosen queen check and the white king coming closer, White takes this defence apart.
key.diagonal: The rook is glued to the black king, on the diagonal. The queen makes a little triangle to pass the move and reaches the Philidor position, the classic winning set-up.
